title: Core Definitions: Ternary and Binary Goldbach
content: The four core predicates establish the formal language for the Goldbach problems. `IsSumOfThreePrimes n` asserts existence of three primes $p,q,r$ with $n = p+q+r$. `WeakGoldbachConjecture` universally quantifies over odd $n>5$. The binary analogues mirror this structure. Lean's existential quantifiers encode the constructive witness form, making these definitions immediately usable for both verification and proof by providing explicit witnesses.
mathContext: $\text{IsSumOfThreePrimes}(n) :\equiv \exists p,q,r \in \mathbb{P},\, n = p + q + r$ and $\text{WeakGoldbach} :\equiv \forall n > 5,\, n \text{ odd} \Rightarrow \text{IsSumOfThreePrimes}(n)$

title: Explicit Witness Verification for Small Cases
content: These five theorems verify the ternary Goldbach property for specific small odd integers by providing explicit prime triples. The pattern `use p, q, r; refine ⟨hp, hq, hr, rfl⟩` follows the existential witness approach. Notably, `decide` is used to automatically verify primality of larger primes (e.g., 5 at line 59, and all three primes for 101). The case $101 = 5 + 43 + 53$ demonstrates that explicit witnesses can be non-trivial — there is no canonical choice, and different decompositions exist.

title: Decidable Instances via Brute-Force Search
content: A `Decidable` instance for `IsSumOfThreePrimes n` enables Lean's kernel to automatically verify or refute any concrete case using `decide`. The implementation uses a brute-force bounded search over triples $(p,q,r) \in [0,n]^3$. Soundness (`isSumOfThreePrimesDecide_sound`) and completeness (`isSumOfThreePrimesDecide_complete`) are fully proved, establishing a verified decision procedure. This pattern — verified decision procedure + `Decidable` instance — is fundamental to computational verification in Lean and enables both positive examples (`IsSumOfThreePrimes 13`) and negative examples (`¬IsSumOfThreePrimes 5`) to be checked automatically.

title: Structural Reduction: Binary Goldbach Implies Ternary
content: This is the most mathematically substantive fully-proved result in the file. The reduction works via parity: every odd $n > 5$ can be written as $n = 3 + (n-3)$, where $n-3$ is even and $> 2$. If the Binary Goldbach Conjecture holds, then $n-3 = p + q$ for primes $p,q$, giving $n = 3 + p + q$ as a ternary representation. The theorem `odd_gt_five_eq_three_plus_even` formalizes the parity arithmetic using `omega`, and `sumOfTwoPrimes_add_three` lifts a binary decomposition to a ternary one. This reduction shows that weak (ternary) Goldbach is a consequence of the still-open strong (binary) Goldbach conjecture.
mathContext: $n > 5,\, n \text{ odd} \Rightarrow n = 3 + (n-3)$ where $n-3$ is even and $> 2$. If $n-3 = p + q$ then $n = 3 + p + q$.

title: Axiomatized Results: Vinogradov and Helfgott
content: The two central axioms capture historical analytic number theory breakthroughs that lie beyond the scope of current Lean formalization. `vinogradov_ternary_goldbach` (1937) gives existence of a threshold $N_0$ above which all odd integers have ternary representations — Vinogradov's proof via exponential sums was groundbreaking but his $N_0$ was effectively uncomputable. `helfgott_weak_goldbach` (2013) asserts the conjecture unconditionally for all $n > 5$; Helfgott's proof spans two papers totaling ~130 pages of analytic estimates. The theorem `weak_goldbach` simply applies the Helfgott axiom, providing the named interface to the main result.
mathContext: $\exists N_0,\, \forall n > N_0,\, n \text{ odd} \Rightarrow n = p+q+r$ (Vinogradov 1937); $\forall n > 5,\, n \text{ odd} \Rightarrow n = p+q+r$ (Helfgott 2013)

title: Vinogradov's Circle Method: Infrastructure and Asymptotic
content: The circle method — developed by Hardy, Littlewood, and Ramanujan in 1918–1920 and refined by Vinogradov — is the central tool in additive prime number theory. The exponential sum $S(\alpha) = \sum_{p \leq N} e(p\alpha)$ where $e(x) = e^{2\pi ix}$, is the Fourier transform of the prime indicator on $[1,N]$. The number of ternary representations $r_3(n)$ equals $\int_0^1 S(\alpha)^3 e(-n\alpha)\,d\alpha$. The method splits this integral into major arcs (near rationals $a/q$ with $q$ small, where $S(\alpha)$ is large and evaluable) and minor arcs (where $|S(\alpha)|$ is small by Vinogradov's bound). The axiomatized asymptotic $r_3(n) \sim \frac{1}{2}S(n)\frac{n^2}{(\log n)^3}$ encapsulates this analysis, where $S(n)$ is the singular series encoding Euler product local corrections.
mathContext: $r_3(n) = \int_0^1 S(\alpha)^3 e(-n\alpha)\,d\alpha,\quad S(\alpha) = \sum_{p \leq N} e^{2\pi i p\alpha},\quad r_3(n) \sim \tfrac{1}{2}\mathfrak{S}(n)\cdot\frac{n^2}{(\log n)^3}$

title: Schnirelmann Density and the Additive Basis Theorem
content: Schnirelmann (1930) introduced a combinatorial approach to additive problems by defining the density $\sigma(A) = \inf_{n \geq 1} |A \cap [1,n]|/n$ for sets $A \subseteq \mathbb{N}$. His key theorem: if $\sigma(A) > 0$, then $A$ is an additive basis of finite order (every sufficiently large integer is a sum of boundedly many elements of $A$). Schnirelmann proved the set of sums of two primes has positive density, yielding the first unconditional result that every large integer is a bounded sum of primes — though the bound (estimated in the hundreds) was far from optimal. The cascade of results formalized here — Ramaré (6 primes, 1995), Tao (5 primes, 2012), Helfgott (3 primes for odd, 2013) — traces the subsequent dramatic improvements.

title: Chen's Theorem, the Goldbach Comet, and Lévy's Conjecture
content: This section formalizes the rich structure of the gap between weak and binary Goldbach. Chen's theorem (1966, published 1973) — every sufficiently large even $n = p + P_2$ where $P_2$ is prime or semiprime — is the deepest unconditional result toward binary Goldbach and uses the large sieve. The `IsP2` predicate captures this. The Hardy-Littlewood asymptotic $G(n) \sim 2C_2 \prod_{p|n, p>2} \frac{p-1}{p-2} \cdot \frac{n}{(\log n)^2}$ predicts the number of binary representations, with the twin prime constant $C_2 \approx 0.6602$. Lévy's conjecture ($n = p + 2q$) is strictly stronger than weak Goldbach: if true, it immediately gives ternary Goldbach (since $p + 2q = p + q + q$), and it is verified here for the small cases 7, 9, 11.
mathContext: $\text{Chen}: n = p + P_2$ (large even $n$); $G(n) \sim 2C_2 \prod_{p | n,\, p > 2}\frac{p-1}{p-2}\cdot\frac{n}{(\log n)^2}$; $C_2 = \prod_{p > 2}\left(1 - \frac{1}{(p-1)^2}\right) \approx 0.6602$
